events.text: Before you, there is a bowl of rice. Then there are fingers: thin, tired, rolling a few spilled grains together, round and round, on the attic floor. Four legs. A head. A tail. A little trunk, pulled out with a fingernail. Then a breath, warm, smelling of old rice and prayer. The fingers stop. Somebody very hungry is looking at you, and laughing under his breath.

choices.text: Wriggle

effects.log: You wriggle, all four legs at once. The monk nearly drops you. "Oh," he says. "Oh no. Oh, Buddha." Then he laughs, quietly, so the house below will not hear, until he has to wipe his eyes.

choices.text: Lie still and look

effects.log: You lie still on his palm and look. Lamp. Thatch. A face with no hair and too many bones. He looks back. "You are awake," he says, very softly, as if to himself. "I only wanted something to talk to."

choices.text: Lift your little trunk toward the lamp

effects.log: You lift your trunk, the size of a rice grain, toward the light. The monk holds his breath. "Not the lamp," he whispers. "That is fire. Never the fire." He tucks your tail into his palm, away from it, and you learn your first thing.

events.text: The hatch lifts. A head and shoulders come up the ladder with a bowl of rice: the keeper of the house, who hides the monk for nothing, with a reward posted on the village gate. {npc} sets down the bowl, sees you on the monk's palm, and stops.

choices.text: Walk across the floor to the bowl

effects.log: You walk, wobbling, across the boards toward the smell of rice. {npc} watches you come the whole way, and then puts one finger down in front of you, like a bridge. You climb it. "Well," {he} says. "Another mouth."

choices.text: Hide behind the monk's knee

effects.log: You hide. The monk explains, badly. {npc} listens to all of it, then says only, "Does it eat?" Nobody knows yet. {He} leaves a few extra grains on the edge of the bowl, just in case.

events.text: Every evening the bowl, and every evening the monk eats slowly and spills a few grains, and every evening you watch the spilled grains and understand something. You are made of that. Of what fell from a hungry man's bowl.

choices.text: Eat a spilled grain

effects.log: You eat one. It goes into you like coming home. But it does not make you more. Rice, you learn, is what you are, not what you grow on.

choices.text: Push the spilled grains back to the monk

effects.log: You push them back across the floor with your trunk, one by one. The monk stops chewing. "You give it back," he says. "Well. You did not get that from me." He eats them, and looks less hungry for a moment.

events.text: Breathing. You did not know you did it until tonight, when the monk is asleep and you lie on his chest and go up and down with it, and notice you go up and down by yourself too. The lamp gutters. Somewhere below, metal clinks: the keepers putting away the supper spoons. Your trunk turns toward the sound before you can stop it.

choices.text: Follow the clink down the ladder

effects.log: You go down the ladder, rung by rung, which takes an hour. In the kitchen there is a spoon on the shelf, bright and cold and smelling of everything you want. You touch it with your trunk. Then you go back up. Not yet. But now you know.

choices.text: Stay on the monk's chest and listen

effects.log: You stay. Up and down. Up and down. Toward dawn the monk wakes, finds you there, and does not move for a long time so as not to tip you off.

events.text: The monk sits by the hatch with his chin on his knees. A reward for every monk caught; a list at the magistrate's; soldiers in the next valley. "I will have to go," he tells you. "And you are small, and full of needles, and very easy to follow."

choices.text: Climb into his sleeve

effects.log: You climb into his sleeve and refuse to come out. He tries twice. Then he sighs, and gives up, and you go to sleep against his wrist.

choices.text: Look at the keepers' house below, then back at him

effects.log: You look down through the gap in the boards at the house that feeds you both. The monk follows your look. "Yes," he says. "If they find me here, they lose everything. You understand that already."

events.text: {npc} comes up with the bowl and sits a while, which {he} never does. {He} looks at you a long time. "Strange," {he} says. "I dreamed once that I hid a monk, in another house, another life. A bowl a day. And then the needle was gone." {He} laughs at the thought, and holds out a finger, and you climb it as if you had always known it.

choices.text: Curl round the finger

effects.log: You curl round it. {npc} goes very still, then very gentle. Whatever {he} dreamed, {he} was kind in it, and is kind now, and something in your rice tail knows the shape of this hand.

choices.text: Touch the finger with your trunk, once, like a bow

effects.log: You touch it with your trunk. {npc} draws a breath. "So," {he} says, "it was not a dream." {He} does not ask anything else. {He} brings a second bowl that night.

events.text: The monk talks to you at night, about the road. "Once," he says, "a house fed me and sent me on. Soup, and new sandals, and they walked me to the edge of the village before the cocks. I left them three grains on the step, pressed into a shape. Like you. I wonder what became of them." You think you know. Something in you remembers a doorstep, and a gate latch.

choices.text: Tell him, the only way you can: eat a latch

effects.log: That night you go down and eat the latch of the keepers' gate, very neatly, and leave it hanging open to the road. In the morning the monk sees it, and goes quite pale, and then laughs.

choices.text: Lie against his hand and listen

effects.log: You lie against his hand. He tells the story twice. Both times you feel a little warmer, as if you had been fed by those people too.

events.text: The keepers' sewing cushion lives on a low chest by the window: silk, stuffed with hair, stuck full of the house's needles. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever smelled. Cold, sharp, clean, like a mountain stream with teeth.

choices.text: Climb the chest

effects.log: You climb the chest by its brass corner, which tastes wonderful, and sit on the cushion among the needles like a frog on a lily pad. You do not eat. Yet. You only breathe it.

choices.text: Watch the hands that sew

effects.log: You watch from the shadows as the mother of the house sews: the needle goes in and out, catching the lamp. It is the thing you want most in the world.

events.text: The needle. One needle, alone on the cushion, the others put away. Hungry is a new word and you have just learned it.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: You take it in your trunk and swallow it, point first. It goes down like cold water, and it stays, a straight bright line inside your rice, and you are more than you were. Your first needle.

choices.text: Eat it slowly, from the eye

effects.log: You start from the eye and eat it slowly, like a noodle. It takes all night. By dawn there is a bright line of steel in you, and you have learned the taste of patience as well as iron.

events.text: After the needle, the scissors. They are the keepers' only pair, iron, with a loose rivet, and they are lying open on the cushion like a mouth.

choices.text: Eat the scissors

effects.log: You eat them, rivet and all. It takes three nights. The house searches for a week. There is steel showing through your grains now, like a fish under ice.

choices.text: Eat only the loose rivet

effects.log: You eat only the rivet. The scissors fall into two halves. The mother of the house finds them, frowns, and has the smith put in a new rivet. You eat that one too, a month later. A little at a time.

events.text: The mother of the house finds you on the cushion with the tip of the last darning needle sticking out of your trunk. You freeze. So does she. Her hand stays where it is, above you, for a long, long moment.

choices.text: Swallow the rest of the needle

effects.log: You swallow it. Gulp. Her mouth falls open, and then she laughs, and laughs, until she has to sit down on the floor and cry, and nobody else in the house can work out why.

choices.text: Spit the needle out into her palm

effects.log: You spit it out into her palm, wet and a little bent. She looks at it, and at you. "Keep it," she says at last, and puts it back on the cushion for you. From then on there is always one needle left out.

events.text: A child of the house, small, solemn, has found you under the sewing chest. And the child does something you were not expecting: holds out the whole needle-case, open, and pushes it under the chest toward you. As if the child had done this before. As if, somewhere, a child always does.

choices.text: Eat the needles one by one

effects.log: You eat them one by one, crunch, crunch, like pine nuts, and the child watches every one. When you are done you sit back and look at the child, and the child nods, satisfied, as if a promise had been kept.

choices.text: Take one, and push the case back

effects.log: You take one needle and push the rest back. The child stares at the case, and then at you, and smiles. "You are polite this time," the child says, and does not know why.

events.text: Candlelight. Rice cakes on a low table. A voice, very tired, talking to you about someone who is dead: how they laughed, how they burned the rice once and blamed the cat. You are a little lump of dough, still warm from the fingers that pressed you, and you are listening.

choices.text: Listen all night

effects.log: You listen all night. Toward dawn the voice stops, and the widowed one who made you puts their head down on the table and sleeps. You sit by the candle, guarding them, which is a thing you decided to do.

choices.text: Nudge the hand with your trunk

effects.log: You nudge the hand. It stops in the middle of a word. Then it strokes you, once, with one finger, very carefully, as if you might come apart.

events.text: The hemp-sewing needle lies in the basket. It is thick and plain and a little rusty, for sewing mourning clothes. It is the thing you want most in the world.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: You eat it. It goes down hard, rust and all, and stays, and you are heavier. In the morning the widowed one searches the basket, then looks at you, and does not say anything at all.

choices.text: Wait until it is given

effects.log: You sit by the basket and wait. On the third night the widowed one sees you looking, and sighs, and holds it out. You take it gently. It tastes better given.

events.text: The in-laws have come for the end of the mourning. The fire tongs are gone, the knife, the iron of the well bucket. The shaman they brought says the dead one's soul is restless. They want the little dough thing burned. They are building the fire in the yard.

choices.text: Hide in the rice-cake basket

effects.log: You hide among the rice cakes, white on white. They search everywhere but the offerings, which would be rude to the dead. The widowed one carries you out under the cloth when they leave.

choices.text: Walk out into the yard and look at them

effects.log: You walk out into the yard, small as you are, and stand in front of the fire and look up at them all. Nobody moves. Then the widowed one picks you up and says, "Not this one," in a voice the family has never heard. They go home.

events.text: A monk comes begging at the gate, thin, hunted, with a staff too old for him. The widowed one, who made you, is his sister, it turns out. They hold each other a long time. Then the monk sees you, and laughs. "So you made one too," he says. "Mine was rice."

choices.text: Climb onto his staff

effects.log: You climb onto the staff and sit at the top like a bird. The monk looks at you along it. "Good," he says. "Then I have someone to talk to in the attic." The widowed one hides him there, a bowl a day, and you go up and down the ladder between them.

choices.text: Stay in your maker's hand

effects.log: You stay in the hand that made you. The monk nods. "Quite right," he says. He hides in the attic all the same, and you are the one who carries him the spilled grains, one at a time, which takes all evening.

events.text: At the mourning table, at the anniversary rite, the widowed one sets out the rice cakes and, beside them, a little row of nails, neat as offerings. "I do not know why," they say to you. "I dreamed of a dough beast and a row of nails, long before you. In another life, perhaps."

choices.text: Eat the nails one by one

effects.log: You eat them one by one, gravely, as a rite. The widowed one watches and, for the first time since the funeral, smiles without it hurting.

choices.text: Lay one nail back on the table

effects.log: You eat all but one and lay that one on the table, for the dead. The widowed one covers their mouth with both hands.

events.text: Spoons are better than needles. Thicker. Brass, some of them, which tastes of autumn. The keepers have six: one for each mouth, and one for guests. Every night one fewer.

choices.text: Eat a spoon a night

effects.log: A spoon a night. In a week the family eats with wooden ones and nobody says a word, the way a family does not speak of a debt. You are bigger now, and you clink when you walk.

choices.text: Eat only the guest spoon

effects.log: You eat only the guest spoon, which no one has used in a year. Nobody notices for a month. When they do, they laugh: no guests, no spoon.

events.text: On the shelf, apart from everything, a brass bowl: old, dented, polished. The grandmother of the house was married with it and has eaten from it every day for fifty years. It smells of the best thing in the world.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: You eat it. It is the best thing you have ever eaten. In the morning the grandmother looks at the empty place on the shelf and says nothing, and eats from a clay bowl, and does not look at you all day. You feel your tail go cold.

choices.text: Lick it, once, and leave it

effects.log: You lick the rim, once, and leave it. That evening the grandmother finds a little wet mark on her bowl and, for no reason anyone can see, gives you the scrapings of the rice pot.

events.text: The father of the house smokes a long pipe in the evenings with a brass bowl and an iron stem, and taps it out on the step. You have been watching that pipe for a week.

choices.text: Eat the iron stem, leave the bowl

effects.log: You eat the stem. He finds the brass bowl on the step with no stem and stares at it for an evening, and then, for the first time in years, does not smoke. The house says he looks better for it.

choices.text: Eat the whole pipe

effects.log: You eat it all. He searches the house and the yard and the village, and comes back at dark and sits on the step with nothing in his hands. You feel it in your tail.

events.text: The rice chest is warm and smells of what you are made of. You sleep in it now, curled on the rice, clinking. Tonight a small child of the house finds you there, and holds up the last brass spoon in the house, the child's own.

choices.text: Take it

effects.log: You take it. The child laughs and claps. Then the child has nothing to eat with at supper and cries. You climb into the child's lap and stay there all evening, which is the only thing you know how to give.

choices.text: Push it back into the small hand

effects.log: You push it back with your trunk. The child looks at it, puzzled, then puts it in the rice chest beside you, as if to keep you company. You leave it there. It is the only spoon in the house you never eat.

events.text: Somebody in this house has always known about you, from the very first night, and has never said a word. You can tell by the way the iron things are left about: a bent nail on the step, a broken hinge by the chest, put there for you. The way you leave grain for a sparrow.

choices.text: Eat only what is left out

effects.log: You eat only what is left out for you. The house keeps its iron, and you keep its secret, and the secret keeps both of you.

choices.text: Leave a bent nail on the step in return

effects.log: You leave a nail on the step, bent into a little shape like a trunk. In the morning it is gone, picked up by whoever has kept your secret. You never find out who. It is enough.

events.text: Torches at the gate. Soldiers, six of them, with a list. Someone has talked. They want the monk. You are under the kitchen floor, in the cold flue of the ondol, where the smoke goes in winter, and above you boots cross the boards.

choices.text: Stay in the flue and do not clink

effects.log: You do not clink. For an hour, every bit of iron in you holds still. The boots go away. You come out black with old soot, and the monk, coming down the ladder at dawn, laughs at you until he coughs.

choices.text: Eat the iron cap off a soldier's spear-butt

effects.log: A spear-butt rests on the floor right above your flue, its iron cap in reach. You eat it. The soldier swears, looks for it, blames the man beside him, and they argue all the way out of the gate.

events.text: The captain looks up at the attic hatch. Up there is the monk. The hatch has an iron lock, and the captain has called for the key.

choices.text: Climb up and eat the lock before the key comes

effects.log: You go up the wall inside, along the beam, and eat the lock out of the hatch from behind, every pin and spring. When the key comes there is nothing to put it in, and the hatch is fixed in place by its own swollen wood. The captain gives up at dawn.

choices.text: Run across the yard to draw them off

effects.log: You run out across the moonlit yard, clinking as loud as you can, and every torch turns. A soldier shouts "Rat!" and they chase you through the jar terrace for an hour, and break three soy jars, and forget the hatch.

events.text: They are gone. The keepers sit in the kitchen without a lamp. Nobody sleeps. The monk comes down the ladder and kneels to them on the floor, and says he will leave tomorrow.

choices.text: Climb into the monk's lap

effects.log: You climb into his lap and stay there, heavy as a stone. He cannot get up without tipping you off. He does not leave tomorrow.

choices.text: Go and sit by the keepers

effects.log: You go and sit by the keepers, who risked the most. The mother of the house puts a hand on you, absently, the way you touch a dog in a storm.

events.text: The soldiers come back, long after you thought they had forgotten, without warning. This time they bring a dog.

choices.text: Stare the dog down

ok.log: The dog finds you in the flue, and you look at it with your small hard eyes, and every needle on you stands up. The dog sits down. Then it lies down. Then it whines to go home, and the soldiers, disgusted, take it.

fail.log: The dog gets you by the tail and shakes you, and you clink like a purse, and something in the rice of your tail hurts as nothing iron ever has. It drops you, puzzled. You lie in the flue a long time afterwards. (-6 health)

choices.text: Lie in the cold ash and do not move

effects.log: You lie in the ash. The dog sniffs at the flue mouth, sneezes, and goes off after the cat. The soldiers leave empty-handed.

events.text: The kitchen fire is lit tonight. You watch it from the flue mouth. You remember, from nowhere, being swept into a fire like this by a broom, once, and rolling out the far side with an ember on your back, unhurt. Except that even then you held your tail up and away.

choices.text: Carry an ember out, the way you remember

effects.log: You walk into the firebox and come out with an ember on your back, unhurt, and carry it across the floor, holding your tail high. The keepers stare. The ember goes into the cold stove and lights it. Fire cannot hurt the iron of you. Only the rice.

choices.text: Curl your tail under you and stay back

effects.log: You curl your tail under you and stay back. Whatever you remember, you remember that the fire knew where your rice was, and was looking for it.

events.text: The keepers' brother-in-law has come to stay. He sits on the veranda and reads the notice from the village gate, over and over, moving his lips at the part with the money.

choices.text: Watch him

effects.log: You watch him. He goes up the ladder once, when he thinks the house is out, and comes down fast with a face like a man who has found a purse.

choices.text: Eat the iron buckle of his purse

effects.log: You eat the buckle of his purse in the night. His coins spill all over the veranda in the morning, and he spends the day picking them out of the cracks and swearing, and has no time for ladders.

events.text: He has gone to the magistrate. Before dawn. You heard the gate. The monk has not woken.

choices.text: Wake the monk

effects.log: You wake him by eating the iron clasp of his robe. He sits up, understands at once, and is out of the back window and up the hill before the cocks. When the soldiers come there is only an empty attic and a bowl.

choices.text: Run after the brother-in-law

effects.log: You run after him down the dark road, clinking. He hears you, and turns, and sees two small eyes in the ditch, and runs, the wrong way, into the paddy. By the time he is out the monk is long gone.

events.text: The brother-in-law has his reward anyway, for the information: strings of iron cash, threaded on cord, a weight of them. He walks home with them over his shoulder, past the ditch where you are waiting.

choices.text: Eat the cash off the string

effects.log: You eat the coins off the cord as he walks, one at a time from the bottom, very quietly. He gets home with a long empty string and a face that will be funny for a hundred years.

choices.text: Let him keep it

effects.log: You let him go. Money for a monk sits badly in a house. Within a year he has lost it all at the market on a bad ox. You did not have to do anything.

events.text: Word comes that the soldiers caught a monk on the hill road, a different one, and are taking him to the county town in a cart.

choices.text: Follow the cart

effects.log: You follow it two days, and on the second night eat the cart's linchpins and the lock on the cage. In the morning the wheels come off and the cage door is open and the monk is gone. You never learn his name.

choices.text: Stay with the keepers

effects.log: You stay. You cannot save everyone. The keepers need you; there are soldiers on the roads. You sit by the gate all night and listen to the cart wheels going away.

events.text: The brother-in-law comes back, poorer, older, and sits on the veranda again. He sees you in the yard. "You," he says. "You ate my money."

choices.text: Cough up one coin at his feet

effects.log: You cough up one coin, a little bent, at his feet. He stares at it, and then at you, and then, against all expectation, laughs. "Fair," he says. "Fair. One coin is about what it was worth."

choices.text: Turn your back on him

effects.log: You turn your back. He sits there a long time. In the morning he has left, and the gate is shut neatly behind him.

events.text: There is something about the brother-in-law's face. You have seen it before, you are sure: in another house, another life, at another gate, walking a monk to the magistrate at dawn. Only then the face was ashamed afterwards. This one is not, yet.

choices.text: Follow him to the magistrate's gate, and wait

effects.log: You follow him, and wait outside the gate. When he comes out with the cash, you are sitting in the road. He stops. You look at him. He puts the cash down in the dust, very slowly, and walks back the way he came. Some faces learn faster the second time.

choices.text: Eat the reward notice off the village gate

effects.log: You eat the nails that hold the notice to the gate, and it blows away into the paddy. No notice, no reward, no reason. He stands at the gate for a long time, looking at four little holes.

events.text: The monk has fled up to a cave on the ridge above the village, and you with him. The cave has a door: a plank, on two old iron hinges, put there by some hermit long dead. The monk sits in the doorway and says the ridge feels strange. As if it were breathing.

choices.text: Eat the hinges

effects.log: You eat the hinges. The plank falls flat. The monk looks at it and says, "Well, now everyone can see in." But the hinges were the best iron you have tasted, old and patient, and something under the ridge seems to sigh.

choices.text: Put your ear to the cave floor

effects.log: You put your ear to the rock. It is breathing. Long, slow, enormous, like the sea. Somewhere far under you something is asleep, and in pain.

events.text: The monk's rice pot is iron. It is the only pot he has. He cooks his one meal a day in it, on three stones, and you have been looking at it for a month.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: You eat it. The monk comes back from the stream with water and finds the three stones and nothing on them. He sits down on the ground and laughs until he weeps, and then cooks his rice in a hollow log, badly, for a year.

choices.text: Leave it, and eat the ladle instead

effects.log: You eat only the ladle. He stirs with a stick after that and says it tastes better. It does not.

events.text: Night. The clouds over the ridge part, and something in them opens: an eye, blue-green, larger than the village, looking down at the cave. At you. A voice like the sea in a cave says: "What are you, that eats my ridge?"

choices.text: Stand very still

effects.log: You stand still. The eye considers you for a long time. Then it closes, slowly, and the clouds close over it, and you are let go. You will never be so small again in your life, or feel so.

choices.text: Answer: I eat iron. Only iron.

effects.log: You do not have a voice yet. But you lift your trunk and the eye understands. "Only iron," says the sea. "Then there is iron in my ridge you could eat, little thing. Old iron. Driven in to hurt me."

choices.text: Bristle every needle at it

effects.log: You bristle. The eye seems amused. A claw comes down out of the cloud, just the tip of it, to flick you off the ridge, and you bite it. A sliver of dragon-claw goes down into you like a cold star. The eye blinks. Then it laughs, like thunder far off, and goes.

events.text: The eye comes back. "There is iron in me," says the voice. "Stakes. Men drove them in to cut my veins. They ache. Eat them, and I will owe you."

choices.text: Agree

effects.log: You agree. The voice tells you where: the saddle of the ridge, under the third pine, where the grass grows thin. The eye closes, satisfied.

choices.text: Ask what it is

effects.log: You ask. "A dragon," it says, "of the east. Nobody has asked me that in a hundred years. They usually run." Then it tells you about the stakes.

events.text: The sliver of claw you swallowed sits in you like a cold star. It does not digest. On stormy nights it hums, and far off over the ridge the dragon's thunder answers it.

choices.text: Keep it

effects.log: You keep it. Some iron is not for growing. It is for remembering who you bit.

choices.text: Cough it up on the ridge, and leave it

effects.log: You cough it up on the highest rock. In the morning it is gone, and that night the rain on the ridge is warm and gentle, as if someone were saying: fair enough.

events.text: Under the third pine, where the grass grows thin, the first stake: a long bar of black iron, rusted, driven deep into the ridge a hundred years ago by men with a compass and a grudge. You put your trunk on it.

choices.text: Pull it out and eat it like barley sugar

effects.log: You pull, and it comes, and you eat it like barley sugar, rust and all. As the last of it goes down, the whole ridge breathes out, long and slow, and the pines shiver. Somewhere above, in the mist, something enormous unclenches.

choices.text: Dig round it first, so the earth is not torn

effects.log: You dig round it with your claws, carefully, an inch at a time, so the ridge is not torn worse. It takes all night. The dragon watches the whole time. At dawn you lift it out whole and eat it, and the earth closes over the hole like a healed cut.

events.text: There are more stakes. Eight, nine, all down the spine of the ridge, each under a thin-grassed spot. The dragon's voice tells you where. Nobody is poorer for any of them. It is iron nobody will miss, given freely.

choices.text: Eat them all, one a night

effects.log: One a night, nine nights. Each time, the ridge breathes easier. On the ninth night it rains, warm, out of a clear sky, and the paddies below fill.

choices.text: Save the last one for the dragon to see

effects.log: You eat eight and leave the last for the dragon to watch. It comes down out of the cloud, coil after coil, closer than it has ever come, and watches you pull the last stake. "Thank you," it says, which dragons do not say.

events.text: Surveyors come back to the ridge with new stakes and a compass. By morning every stake is gone. They try again. By morning, gone. On the third night one of them sits up with a lantern, and sees you.

choices.text: Eat his lantern's iron frame

effects.log: You eat the frame of his lantern while he watches. The paper falls round the candle and the candle goes out, and in the dark he hears you chewing. The surveyors leave the province.

choices.text: Sit and look at him until he goes

effects.log: You sit and look at him. He looks at you. Toward dawn he packs up his stakes and his compass and walks down off the ridge without a word, and never comes back.

events.text: The keepers' house has no iron left. But the door is open, and the night is warm, and down the lane there are twenty kitchens.

choices.text: Go out of the door

effects.log: You go out of the door. Twenty kitchens. Knives on hooks, brass bowls on shelves, a hoe leaning by a woodshed. You come home at dawn so heavy you can hardly climb the step.

choices.text: Go out, but only to the rubbish heaps

effects.log: You go out to the rubbish heaps behind the houses: a cracked pot, a broken sickle, rusted nails. Nobody is poorer. It takes longer.

events.text: The village wakes to empty hooks. People stand in their doorways in their sleeping clothes and look at the places where the knives were. There are little round prints in the dust of every kitchen.

choices.text: Watch from under the keepers' veranda

effects.log: You watch. You did not know that a missing knife could make someone sit down on a step and put their face in their hands. You learn it now.

choices.text: Bring one knife back, to the house that wept

effects.log: You find the house where the old man sat down on the step, and that night you cough up his knife on the threshold, wet and a little bent. In the morning he holds it as if it were a child come home.

events.text: The headman has called a shaman. She comes with a drum, a fan and a string of iron bells, and dances in the village square all night to drive out the thief of iron.

choices.text: Eat her bells

effects.log: You creep in among the crowd's feet and eat her bells off the string, one by one, while she dances. By dawn she is dancing in silence. She stops, looks at the empty string, and sits down, laughing helplessly. The village is not reassured.

choices.text: Sit at the edge of the square and watch

effects.log: You sit at the edge of the light and watch her dance. She sees you. She does not stop dancing, but she dances, for the rest of the night, toward you, as if introducing you to something.

events.text: The shaman comes looking for you, alone, at dusk. She finds you under the keepers' veranda and squats down. "You are not a ghost," she says. "You are a mouth. Somebody made you. Who?"

choices.text: Look up at the ridge where the monk is

effects.log: You look at the ridge. She follows the look and nods slowly. "A monk," she says. "Of course. They make things when they are lonely." She gives you a broken bell, and goes, and tells the village the thief has moved on.

choices.text: Eat the iron pin in her hair

effects.log: You eat her hairpin. Her hair falls down. She looks at you through it a long time, and then says, "Rude," and goes, and tells the village you are a demon, which is half right.

events.text: The village has stopped hanging its knives on hooks. They hang them in the rafters now, on rope, which you cannot reach. Someone has left a pile of scrap by the well instead, as if to say: this, not those.

choices.text: Eat the scrap and leave the rafters alone

effects.log: You eat the scrap. The rafters keep their knives. A sort of treaty, and you keep it.

choices.text: Climb the rafters anyway

effects.log: You climb the rafters and eat every knife. The village wakes to cut ropes and nothing. The scrap pile by the well stays untouched. Nobody leaves you one again.

events.text: The grown-ups are afraid of you. The children are not. They find you sleeping on the threshing floor at noon and sit in a ring round you and argue about whether you are a dog.
events.arc: The Children Who Feed It Nails

choices.text: Wake up and sneeze at them

effects.log: You sneeze. Needles rattle. The children scream with joy and scatter and come straight back. You have, it seems, made friends.

choices.text: Pretend to be asleep

effects.log: You pretend to be asleep. A girl puts her hand on your trunk, very bravely. You let her. By the end of the afternoon you are a pillow for four children.

events.text: The girl who touched your trunk has decided you need a name. She tries several. She settles on one that is very silly: the name of a sweet the pedlar sells at New Year. She says it very seriously, three times.
events.arc: The Children Who Feed It Nails

choices.text: Answer to it

effects.log: You lift your head when she says it. She is so delighted she shouts it all over the village. From then on every child calls you by it, and it is the most foolish name a beast ever had, and you like it.

choices.text: Ignore it, with dignity

effects.log: You ignore it with great dignity. She says it again, and again, and on the tenth time your tail twitches. She sees. It is your name now.

events.text: The children bring you nails. They pull them out of fences, find them in the road, prise them from the old shrine. One at a time, held out on flat palms, the way you feed a horse.
events.arc: The Children Who Feed It Nails

choices.text: Take each one gently

effects.log: You take each one with the very tip of your trunk, so gently that not one child is scratched. They line up. You are fed a hundred nails a day, and every one is given.

choices.text: Tell them, somehow, not the shrine nails

effects.log: When a boy holds out a nail from the shrine you turn your head away. He puzzles over it, then puts it back. After that the children bring you only the road's nails.

events.text: The girl who named you comes to the threshing floor with something heavy, dragging it: her father's plough, the share of it, the iron part. She has run out of nails.
events.arc: The Children Who Feed It Nails

choices.text: Refuse it

effects.log: You turn your head away and will not take it. She pushes it at you. You lie down on your trunk. At last she drags it home again, crying, and her father, who has been searching all morning, does not ask where she took it.

choices.text: Take it, it is given

effects.log: It is given. You take it. It is the best iron you have had in a year. That spring her father has no plough, and the girl does not come to the threshing floor again.

events.text: The village smith cannot keep up. Every hoe he makes, you eat. Every knife. He works all night with his apprentice on the bellows, and in the morning the rack is bare again. Tonight he sees you at his door.

choices.text: Sit down politely by the scrap heap

effects.log: You sit down by the heap of scrap, very straight, and look at him. He looks at you, and at the scrap, and at his empty rack. "I see," he says.

choices.text: Walk in and look at the rack

effects.log: You walk in and look at the empty rack, and then at him. He picks up his tongs. Then he puts them down. "There is nothing on it," he says. "You saw to that."

events.text: The smith squats in the doorway and talks to you like a man selling an ox. Scrap, every night: the broken, the rusted, the bent, everything the village throws out. In return you leave his rack alone.

choices.text: Accept: lie down on the threshold

effects.log: You lie down on his threshold, which is how you say yes. From that night the scrap is yours and the rack is his, and the smith sleeps for the first time in a month.

choices.text: Eat the anvil

effects.log: You eat his anvil. It takes three nights and he cannot stop you. On the third morning he sits in the ashes of his forge with his hands in his lap and weeps, the way a man weeps for a father. You are heavier than you have ever been, and your tail is cold.

events.text: The bargain holds. The village carries its broken iron to the smith, and the smith carries it out to you. You lie by the forge at night and listen to him hammer, and he talks to you while he works.

choices.text: Listen to him

effects.log: He tells you about iron: how it is dug, how it is smelted, how a plough is folded so it holds an edge. You listen all winter. You are the first beast to know what it eats.

choices.text: Work the bellows with your trunk

effects.log: You work the bellows with your trunk while his apprentice sleeps. The fire roars. He laughs and says he has never had such a strong apprentice, or such a hungry one.

events.text: The smith has no anvil. He hammers on a flat stone, and his ploughs crack. The village goes without. He does not look at you any more when you pass.

choices.text: Cough up iron at his door, as much as you can

effects.log: You cough at his door until you are dizzy: an anvil's weight, near enough, in nails and knives and spoons. He comes out, and looks, and kneels in it. Then he goes to fetch his tongs. He does not thank you. That is fair.

choices.text: Keep away from the smithy

effects.log: You keep away. Some things cannot be put right by staying near them. You hear his hammer on the stone at night, cracking, all winter.

events.text: Spring. Every plough in the valley is gone but one: an old widow's, at the far end of the valley, with a share worn thin by forty years. The spring ploughing is in three days. You can smell it from the ridge.

choices.text: Go down and look at it

effects.log: You go down at dusk. The widow is sitting in the field with both arms round the plough handle, as if it were a person. She has seen you coming.

choices.text: Stay on the ridge

effects.log: You stay on the ridge. But you can still smell it, all night, and all the next day.

events.text: The widow looks at you over the plough handle. She does not run. "Go on, then," she says. "Take it. You have taken everybody else's."

choices.text: Take it

effects.log: You take it. She lets go when you pull. It is thin and old and sweet. She walks home with nothing in her hands. Your tail goes cold to the tip, and stays cold.

choices.text: Lie down beside it, and guard it till the ploughing

effects.log: You lie down beside it. She stares. For three days you lie in the field, and every night she brings you a bent nail, and on the fourth day she ploughs, and you walk home beside her, and she talks to you the whole way.

events.text: The widow ploughs the only furrows in the valley. Neighbours come to borrow her plough, one day each, all down the valley. It is passed from hand to hand for a month. She asks you to walk it from house to house.

choices.text: Carry it in your trunk, house to house

effects.log: You carry it in your trunk to every house in the valley, and never once eat it. It is the hardest month of your life and the proudest.

choices.text: Walk behind it, guarding

effects.log: You walk behind whoever is ploughing, all month. Nobody fears you that spring.

events.text: The widow's furrows are not ploughed. Her field is dry and full of weeds. Once, you see her at the edge of it, scratching at the earth with a stick.

choices.text: Go and scratch the earth beside her with your claws

effects.log: You go and dig beside her with your claws, all day, furrow after furrow, badly. She does not speak to you. At dusk she leaves you a bowl of water. It is not forgiveness. It is a bowl of water.

choices.text: Watch from the treeline

effects.log: You watch from the treeline. Wanting something is not a reason. You learn that now, the hard way, and it costs her, not you.

events.text: The house cat has noticed you. You are small and smell of rice. The cat is crouched by the stove with its tail going.
events.arc: The Cat and the Mouse-Sized Thing

choices.text: Stand your ground

ok.log: It pounces. It bites. Its tooth breaks on the steel inside you with a crack you hear across the kitchen. It backs off, outraged, with its mouth open. You sit there, smug as a needle.

fail.log: It pounces and rolls you across the floor like a ball, and you go under the stove with the cat's paw after you, and lie there clinking with rage. It breaks a claw on you. Neither of you wins. (-3 health)

choices.text: Run under the sewing chest

effects.log: You run. The cat waits by the chest all night. In the morning it is still there, and so are you, and you look at each other with a sort of respect.

events.text: The cat has a broken tooth now, and a grudge. It follows you everywhere, two steps behind, its tail stiff.
events.arc: The Cat and the Mouse-Sized Thing

choices.text: Bring it a fish bone from the rubbish

effects.log: You bring it a fish bone. It sniffs. It eats. It sits down next to you, and does not leave, and from then on it follows you two steps behind in quite a different way.

choices.text: Ignore it

effects.log: You ignore it. It ignores you, harder. After a month you realise it has been chasing the rats away from you the whole time, out of spite.

events.text: A stray dog comes into the yard, big, hungry, nosing at the rice chest where you sleep. The cat gets there first.
events.arc: The Cat and the Mouse-Sized Thing

choices.text: Help the cat

effects.log: You come out bristling, every needle up, beside the cat with its broken tooth. The dog takes one look at a cat and a hedge of needles and goes, fast. The cat washes its paw, very pleased with itself.

choices.text: Let the cat handle it

effects.log: You let the cat handle it. It does. Your guard, it seems, takes its work seriously.

events.text: The rats in the granary can smell you. Not the iron: the rice. Your tail. They come out of the straw in the dark, a dozen of them, noses going.

choices.text: Pull your tail in and bristle

effects.log: You pull your tail under you and stand every needle up. The rats circle. One tries, and gets a nose full of steel, and squeals. They go. You lie awake till dawn with your tail tucked in, learning something.

choices.text: Run

effects.log: You run, and one gets your tail, just the tip, and nibbles. It does not hurt like the iron hurts. It hurts like being forgotten. You get away. Your tail is a little shorter, and you will never let it hang loose again.

events.text: You understand now. Everything of you that is iron, nothing can eat. But the tail is rice, and rice is food, and whatever eats food can eat that.

choices.text: Promise yourself to guard it

effects.log: You promise. From now on your tail is always tucked in, or behind you, or under you. It is the first thing you have ever had to keep safe.

choices.text: Show it to the monk, puzzled

effects.log: You show the monk your bitten tail. He goes very quiet, and strokes it with one finger. "That is the part that is mine," he says. "Keep it."

events.text: You are bigger now, and the rats are still in the granary, eating the keepers' rice. They do not come near you any more.

choices.text: Eat the iron of their holes: the granary nails

effects.log: You eat the loose nails of the granary walls where they get in. The keepers nail new boards. The rats move to the neighbours'. You are not sure that counts as a victory.

choices.text: Sleep across the granary door

effects.log: You sleep across the granary door all winter. Not one rat comes in. The keepers' rice lasts till spring for the first time in years.

events.text: Tonight you try to go down between two floorboards, as you always do, and stick. Too big for the boards. The monk pulls you out by the back legs.

choices.text: Look at yourself in the water bowl

effects.log: You look at yourself in the water bowl: grey, needled, with a trunk and two small hard eyes, and a pale little tail. You do not look like rice any more. You look like what you ate.

choices.text: Shake yourself all over

effects.log: You shake yourself and every needle rattles like a pedlar's tray. The monk covers his ears. Downstairs a keeper drops a pot.

events.text: The attic floor cracks. You are calf-sized, and you did not notice until the beam under you groaned and the monk jumped up and the keepers below shouted.

choices.text: Lie very still until they prop it

effects.log: You lie very still. They prop the beam with a post from the woodshed. The monk sits back against the wall and laughs until he cries. "I made you out of four grains," he says. "Four."

choices.text: Go down the ladder, carefully

effects.log: You go down the ladder. The ladder does not survive. You arrive in the kitchen in a heap of splinters. Nobody is hurt. You sleep in the yard after that.

events.text: You lie in the yard at night, too big for any room of the house, and listen to the keepers sleep. Inside you the needle, the spoons, the knives, the scissors, the iron of the whole village clink when you breathe.

choices.text: Count everything you ate

effects.log: You count it. Every piece. You know exactly whose each was. It is a long list. You resolve to remember it, all of it, always.

choices.text: Sleep

effects.log: You sleep, and dream of mountains made of iron, and wake hungry.

events.text: The monk says you need a name, since you will not stop eating. He tries grand ones and laughs at all of them. In the end he gives you a silly one, the kind you give a thing you made from your own supper, and says it three times.

choices.text: Lift your trunk to it

effects.log: You lift your trunk. That is your name, then. He uses it every day after that, and nobody else in the world knows it.

choices.text: Sneeze

effects.log: You sneeze. He takes it as yes. That is your name, then, whether you like it or not, and you do.

events.text: "Eat less," says the monk, using your name. "I do not say none. You are what you are. Less."

choices.text: Eat less, for a month

effects.log: You eat less for a month. It is very hard. At the end of it the monk gives you his own iron chopsticks, the last thing he owns, and you eat them so slowly that he laughs.

choices.text: Look at him, and eat a spoon

effects.log: You look at him and eat a spoon. He sighs. "Well," he says. "You are young."

events.text: The monk says your name in his sleep. Then, waking, he tells you something strange: "If I am ever gone, and you do not know when to stop, someone may say that name to you. Listen to them."

choices.text: Promise, with your trunk on his hand

effects.log: You lay your trunk on his hand. He nods, and goes back to sleep. You lie awake, saying the name to yourself, so you will know it again anywhere.

choices.text: Ask, the only way you can, where he is going

effects.log: You press against him. "Nowhere," he says. "Yet." You do not believe him, and you are right not to.

events.text: A summer of sutras. The monk chants every evening in the cave, the same words over and over, and you lie across the entrance and listen. The words do not mean anything to you. The rhythm does.

choices.text: Listen until you fall asleep

effects.log: You fall asleep to it, every night. You wake less hungry than you have ever been.

choices.text: Chew in time to the chanting

effects.log: You chew a nail in time to the chant. The monk opens one eye and does not stop. It is, he says afterwards, the best accompaniment he has ever had.

events.text: "Not none," says the monk, after the chanting. "Less." He has said it before. This summer, for the first time, you hear it.

choices.text: Eat only what is broken, all summer

effects.log: All summer you eat only broken things: the bent, the cracked, the rusted. You grow slower. You feel better than you have since the attic.

choices.text: Eat nothing for nine days, to see

effects.log: You eat nothing for nine days. On the ninth the monk feeds you his prayer-bead clasp, laughing. "Less," he says. "I said less. Not this."

events.text: Autumn. The monk's chanting has grown thinner, like his voice. He coughs at night. He asks you to lie closer, for the warmth.

choices.text: Lie closer, and keep still all night

effects.log: You lie against him all night and keep so still that not one needle pricks him. Iron is cold, but you have learned to hold the warmth of the day in you, like a stone in the sun.

choices.text: Go and steal him a quilt from the keepers

effects.log: You go down to the village and come back with a quilt, which you carry very carefully so as not to eat its pins. The monk laughs and coughs and sleeps.

events.text: A burned temple on a hill, roofless, deep in weeds. In the hall, under the sky, sits a buddha of cast iron, as tall as a doorway, older than anyone remembers. It is the most iron you have ever seen in one place. It has a very calm face.

choices.text: Sit down in front of it

effects.log: You sit down in front of it. It looks at you. You look at it. You are both iron, mostly. It is very much calmer about it than you are.

choices.text: Walk round it, sniffing

effects.log: You walk round it three times, sniffing. Old iron, poured all at once, a long time ago, by many hands. It smells of prayer and rain.

events.text: Nobody comes to the burned temple any more. Nobody would miss the iron buddha. It would make you twice what you are.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: You eat it, from the base up, over a month. When the face is all that is left you hesitate a long time. Then you eat that too. You are heavy as a cart of stone. And somewhere in you there is a calm you did not have before, and do not deserve.

choices.text: Guard it

effects.log: You lie down at its feet. You will guard it, you decide, from anyone who would melt it. Nobody comes. You guard it all the same.

events.text: Monks come back to the burned temple: three of them, young, with saws and a cart, to rebuild. They stop at the hall door and stare.

choices.text: Move aside for them

effects.log: You get up and move aside. They come in, very slowly, past you, and bow to the buddha, and then, after a moment, to you. They rebuild the roof that summer. You sleep in the yard.

choices.text: Lie where it was, and let them see the empty hall

effects.log: They see the empty hall and the place where it sat, and then you. One of them sits down on the floor and weeps. The others pray. Nobody chases you. That is worse.

choices.text: Go off into the hills

effects.log: You go off into the hills before they can decide what you are. Some things are better not explained.

events.text: A temple outside Cheongju. Through the window, the most delicious smell you have ever met: hundreds and hundreds of tiny pieces of metal, each the size of a fingernail, each with a character on it, lying in trays. The monks are setting them into a frame, inking them, pressing paper. A book is being made of iron.

choices.text: Put your trunk in at the window

effects.log: Your trunk goes in at the window before you can stop it. A monk looks up, sees it, and freezes with a character in his tweezers. Very slowly, he holds it out to you.

choices.text: Lie down outside and just smell

effects.log: You lie down under the window and breathe it in all day. It smells of ink and bronze and patience. You do not eat. You do not know why.

events.text: A monk with a pair of tweezers is holding out one piece of type to you through the window. One character, cast in metal. The others are shouting at him to stop.

choices.text: Take it, and eat it

effects.log: You take it, and eat it. It is the best thing you have ever tasted, a whole word in one bite. The monks will have to cast it again. You carry one character inside you for the rest of your life, and you never learn what it says.

choices.text: Push it back into his hand

effects.log: You push it back into his palm with the tip of your trunk. He stares at it. Then he sets it into the frame, in its place, and goes on, and the others stop shouting.

events.text: Soldiers on the road to the temple. They have heard there is metal here, a great deal of it, and the county needs arrowheads.

choices.text: Lie across the temple gate

effects.log: You lie across the gate. The soldiers come up the road and see you, ox-sized nearly, every needle up, and stop. Their captain counts his men, counts your needles, and goes back down the road. The book is finished that month.

choices.text: Eat the soldiers' arrowheads first

effects.log: You go down to meet them and eat every arrowhead out of their quivers on the road before they get anywhere near. They go back without arrowheads, which is a hard thing to explain to a county.

events.text: The book is printed. The monks pack the type into boxes, and the boxes into a cart, to hide them in the hills before more soldiers come. The cart has no ox.

choices.text: Pull the cart

effects.log: You pull the cart up into the hills all night, the monks walking beside you, and never once open a box. At dawn they hide it in a cave and bow to you, all of them, as if you were a teacher.

choices.text: Carry the printed books, not the type

effects.log: You carry the printed books in your trunk, wrapped in oilcloth. The type can be cast again. The books are the point. The monks see that you understand, and say nothing, and are amazed.

events.text: Spring, and the village cannot plant. There are no ploughs, no hoes, no sickles. They are inside you. The farmers turn the soil with sharpened sticks, and the earth is hard as a pot, and the children are thin.

choices.text: Watch from the treeline

effects.log: You watch all day from the treeline. This is yours. Nobody else did this.

choices.text: Go down and dig with your claws

effects.log: You go down into the field and dig with your claws beside the farmers. They scatter. Then, slowly, one comes back and digs beside you. By dusk there are furrows, crooked ones.

events.text: The keepers go hungry with the rest. You see the mother of the house dividing a bowl of millet into five. She gives the biggest share to the youngest, and none to herself.

choices.text: Cough up a plough at their door

effects.log: You cough at the keepers' door until a ploughshare comes up, then another, then a hoe. It hurts. It is the first iron you ever gave back. The mother of the house stands in the doorway and does not say anything, and then she does: "Well. Come in out of the cold."

choices.text: Leave the village, so it can forget you

effects.log: You leave the village at night and go up to the old mine on the ridge, where there is iron in the rock that nobody needs. Behind you, the village begins, slowly, to forget.

events.text: The smiths of the market town hear that a valley has no ploughs, and come with carts of new iron, at a price. The village sells its rice seed to buy them.

choices.text: Eat the smiths' carts' iron before they reach the village

effects.log: You go to eat the carts, and stop on the road, looking at them. They are the village's ploughs. They are what you took, come back. You let them pass.

choices.text: Lie by the road and watch the ploughs go by

effects.log: You lie by the road and watch them go by, one cart after another, and never move. A child on the last cart waves at you. You lift your trunk.
